# John DeSouza: blog, full text

> Director of Product Design with 13 years across consumer lending (Best Egg), blockchain infrastructure (Chainlink Labs) and enterprise identity (Auth0). Every post below is one position, with the sources it rests on.

---

## The bottleneck moved and the budget didn’t

- URL: https://john-desouza.com/blog/the-constraint-moved-to-review.html
- Author: John DeSouza
- Published: 2026-09-29
- Topic: Design leadership
- Claim: When agents triple a team’s output the constraint moves to the people who decide whether the work is right, and spending that gain on a deferred hire funds the queue instead of the decision.

A chief product officer published his agent-run team this week. Seven people, an agent each, and each designer producing what three used to. Halfway through he names his own constraint, and a few paragraphs later he says where the savings went.

On September 25, Dan Graves, chief product officer at WitnessAI, [published an account](https://www.cio.com/article/4226177/i-stopped-asking-my-team-to-use-ai-i-asked-them-to-manage-it.html) of how his product team works now. Seven people, each managing a role-based agent with subagents under it. A product design agent called Muffin turns mockups into working code. An orchestrator called PacMan routes tickets. Release velocity doubled. By the team’s own weekly measure, interfaces designed, each user experience designer now produces what three used to.

It’s the most specific writeup of an agent-run product team I’ve read this year, and he’s candid about what broke. Muffin’s early designs “looked right on the surface but used the wrong components and missed our branding”, and developers reworked half the output. A senior designer picked “finish the load animations” off a list of options just to point Muffin at the task, and Muffin started building. That’s a real account, not a case study with the failures sanded off.

The sentence I keep going back to sits in the middle of it. “We’ve since automated the path from specification to ship, which only moved the constraint. The human reviewers are now the bottleneck.”

## Then he says where the money went

Further down the same piece: “Together, these gains have let us defer hiring new staff.”

He’s right on both counts, and the two point opposite ways. The team found its constraint and then spent the surplus everywhere except on it. Output at the designer level went up three times. The number of people who can look at that output and say no stayed at seven.

I don’t read that as carelessness. It’s what a throughput gain feels like from the inside. The queue gets longer at the last step, which is the least visible place for it to get longer, and the savings from not hiring land this quarter while the cost of a thin review lands in something that ships wrong two quarters from now.

## It isn’t one team’s problem

Two days before that piece ran, Qodo published [a Censuswide survey](https://www.qodo.ai/blog/state-of-ai-code-quality-report-2026/) of 500 American software developers and 300 American engineering leaders, all at companies where AI already does real work in the development lifecycle. The two groups answered separate questionnaires and never saw each other’s answers. Asked to name the primary constraint in their delivery pipeline, both picked reviewing and validating AI-generated code, at 26% each. It outranked trusting the output, integration, security and compliance, context retrieval and cost in both samples.

Two audiences with different incentives, one answer. The report’s line for it is that “generation scaled across the entire lifecycle, and verification never scaled with it”. In the same research, 89% of organizations reported an AI-related production incident, and 3.7% of engineering leaders said their current processes are enough to hold quality as agents take on more work.

That’s engineering data. The design version is on the same curve now, because design output goes into the same pipeline. When an agent hands a reviewer finished frontend code with the mockups attached, the reviewer’s problem is the one those 800 people just described.

## Teaching agents to out-review humans

Graves’s answer to his own bottleneck is to push the review down to the agents. His team aggregates everyone’s review questions into a checklist the agents run every time, then asks Claude for other industry review practices and teaches those too. “Eventually, an agent reviews things 100 ways automatically, leaving less that requires a human eye.”

Half of that is right and it’s the half nobody should be arguing with. If a check can be written down as a rule, a person should never run it twice. Component use, contrast, the naming, whether the empty state was drawn at all: that work belongs to an agent running at three in the morning.

The other half files a hundred checks and one decision under the same word. A checklist can tell you the screen conforms. It can’t tell you the screen shouldn’t exist, that the flow asks an applicant for a document they won’t have on a Sunday, or that the answer is correct and still wrong for this customer. Automating the first job doesn’t create capacity for the second. It clears the desk faster and leaves the same people holding the part that was always scarce.

## The hire you already paid for

Box’s [2026 State of AI in the Enterprise](https://blog.box.com/SAI26-agentic-ai-is-here) surveyed 1,640 information technology decision makers across the United States, United Kingdom, France and Japan in early May. 58% expect headcount to rise over the next three years. Among the most mature adopters, 79% do. The companies furthest into this are not the ones planning to be smaller.

So deferring a hire is a choice, and it deserves to be argued as one. A team that triples its output has earned the case for another person who can decide. Making that case is harder than banking the saving, because the deferred hire is a line a finance partner can see and a thin review is not.

## How I plan a team now

I size a team by what it can decide in a week rather than what it can produce. When I ran the whole-library audit of [Best Egg’s design system](https://john-desouza.com/work/agentic-design-system-audit.html), the plan divided at write access: specs and lists to the agent, every edit to the library to one senior product designer, and the order set by who could act. The agent was never the constraint. One read-only run produced 28 fixes with deep links into Figma. Write access was the constraint, and we built the schedule around it instead of finding out later.

Before anyone on my team adds an agent, I ask two things. Who signs this off, and what else is already on that person’s desk. If the answer is someone already at capacity, the agent isn’t adding throughput. It’s adding a queue with their name on it.

Graves knows exactly what his agents cost. He publishes the figure: $2,000 to $5,000 per person per month. The review those agents generate doesn’t appear on any invoice, which is most of the reason it’s the easy thing to defer.

Sources:

- [I stopped asking my team to use AI. I asked them to manage it](https://www.cio.com/article/4226177/i-stopped-asking-my-team-to-use-ai-i-asked-them-to-manage-it.html)
- [The 2026 State of AI Code Quality Report](https://www.qodo.ai/blog/state-of-ai-code-quality-report-2026/)
- [Agentic AI is here. The leading edge is capturing most of the value](https://blog.box.com/SAI26-agentic-ai-is-here)
- [Agentic design system audit and remediation](/work/agentic-design-system-audit.html)

## Disclose the review, not the tool

- URL: https://john-desouza.com/blog/disclose-the-review-not-the-tool.html
- Author: John DeSouza
- Published: 2026-09-28
- Topic: Where product design is going
- Claim: Naming the tool isn’t a quality signal, because the same disclosure penalty lands on a master and a beginner. What a client can act on is the record of what was checked and what came back wrong, and no disclosure policy asks anyone to write that down.

Fifty-eight percent of creative professionals have used AI on client work without telling the client. The industry reads that as a discipline problem and is busy writing better rules for when to say the word. The word was never the part worth having.

Nielsen Norman Group published a framework last week for deciding when to tell people AI was involved in your work. Taylor Dykes calls it [PACED](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/disclose-ai-paced/): policy, audience, context, expectations and degree of use.

It’s careful work and it names the awkward part honestly. People say they want disclosure and then think less of the person who gives it.

I’d use that framework tomorrow. I also think the question underneath it’s set up wrong, and a good framework built on a bad question inherits the problem.

“AI was used here” is a fact about a tool. Nobody on the receiving end is asking about the tool.

## The label costs something and says nothing

Envato surveyed 1,780 creative professionals for [Beyond Adoption](https://elements.envato.com/learn/ai-trend-report). Fifty-eight percent have used AI on client work without telling the client. Only 31% always disclose.

The more interesting number is the reason. Of the people who said nothing, 48% said they don’t see why they should have to disclose every tool. That gets read as a rationalization. It’s half right.

Nobody itemizes Figma, the stock license, the plugin or the Slack thread where the idea actually came from. A tool name has never told a client whether the work is any good.

And the penalty for saying this particular tool name is measurable. Dykes cites the studies: ratings drop as the disclosed share of AI involvement goes up. The research Florida International University [wrote up](https://news.fiu.edu/2026/artists-and-writers-are-often-hesitant-to-disclose-theyve-collaborated-with-ai-and-those-fears-may-be-justified) from Joel Carnevale, Anand Benegal and Lynne Vincent is the part that should stop people. Listeners marked a composition down when they were told AI was involved, and the hit landed whether they believed the piece came from Hans Zimmer or from a first-year music student.

The same penalty fell on a master and a beginner.

A signal that can’t tell those two apart isn’t carrying information about the work. It’s carrying a reaction to a category, and we’re building policy on top of it.

## Provenance is not review

[Article 50](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/50/) of the EU AI Act became applicable on August 2, 2026. Synthetic audio, image, video and text have to be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. Deepfakes get disclosed. A chatbot has to say what it is.

That’s provenance and it’s worth having. It answers whether a machine made the pixels, which is a real question for a voice in an ad or a face in a video.

It doesn’t answer the question a client, a reviewer or a design lead is actually asking. That question is whether anyone competent looked at this, and what they were looking for.

## The review is happening off the books

In [AI in Design 2026](https://stateofaidesign.com/chapters/craft), the survey Designer Fund and Foundation Capital ran with 900 designers across 60 countries, 80% say they rely on their own quality judgment over the model’s. Half have pushed AI-generated code to production. Forty percent claim full ownership of AI-assisted work and another 43% say it’s mostly theirs.

So the review exists. It happens in one person’s head, it takes real skill, and it leaves nothing behind that anybody else can inspect.

Patrick Neeman got close to this in [Craft Still Matters](https://aiforux.substack.com/p/craft-still-matters-but-its-not-about), arguing that you describe your standards and keep humans reviewing. What I’d add is that the describing has to land somewhere a reader can find it.

## What I write instead

Nothing I hand over carries the words “AI-assisted”. The line I write instead says what I checked and what came back wrong.

Three sentences, at the top, before the work: here’s what I checked this against, here’s where it failed, here’s what I changed. If I can’t write those three sentences, naming the tool doesn’t rescue the handoff, and naming the tool is the only thing most disclosure policies ask me for.

I ran a whole-library audit at Best Egg and wrote the crawler’s rules myself. The rules are the reason anyone could argue with the output. A flag was checkable because the rule behind it was on paper, which meant the interesting conversation was about the rule and not about the crawler.

In an interview I ask for one piece of work and the thing the model got wrong on it. Not whether they use the tools. What the first answer was, why they threw it out and what they held it up against. A candidate who can’t answer that has been shipping unreviewed work, and no disclosure label would have told me.

## Who stays quiet, and why

Dykes is right that being caught out hurts more than telling people yourself, and that’s a good reason to disclose when policy is pointed at you. It’s also why disclosure gets heard as a confession. A confession is a bad container for a claim about quality.

The Envato rates break along exposure. Agency and studio owners disclose least at 28%, behind freelancers at 31% and in-house designers at 35%. Europe is highest at 39% and the Middle East and Africa lowest at 22%.

The people with the most staff and the most to lose say the least. That’s what a label looks like when it carries risk and no upside.

You don’t fix that with a better decision tree about when to say the word. You fix it by changing what gets said, from a fact about the tool to a record of the judgment. A record gets more useful as the tools spread. The tool name is heading for describing everything, and a label that describes everything sorts nothing.

Fifty-eight percent are already not saying it. Arguing them into compliance is a smaller win than it looks. What a client can act on is the check, and not one of the frameworks in this argument asks anyone to write the check down.

Sources:

- [When Should You Disclose AI Use? The PACED Framework](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/disclose-ai-paced/)
- [Beyond Adoption: The State of AI in Creative Work 2026](https://elements.envato.com/learn/ai-trend-report)
- [Artists and writers are often hesitant to disclose they've collaborated with AI](https://news.fiu.edu/2026/artists-and-writers-are-often-hesitant-to-disclose-theyve-collaborated-with-ai-and-those-fears-may-be-justified)
- [Article 50](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/50/)
- [Craft, AI in Design 2026](https://stateofaidesign.com/chapters/craft)
- [Craft Still Matters But It's All About Outcomes, Not Pixels](https://aiforux.substack.com/p/craft-still-matters-but-its-not-about)

## A name match is not a verdict

- URL: https://john-desouza.com/blog/a-name-match-is-not-a-verdict.html
- Author: John DeSouza
- Published: 2026-09-27
- Topic: Fintech, web3 and trust
- Claim: A payee name check answers one narrow question, and the screen reporting it’s where a bank quietly answers a much bigger one on the payer’s behalf.

Payee name checking is now running on almost every instant payment in Britain and every euro credit transfer in Europe. The rulebooks specify the message down to the response code. What the person reads is left to whoever writes the strings.

On September 20 the European Payments Council’s [Verification of Payee rulebook](https://www.europeanpaymentscouncil.eu/sites/default/files/kb/file/2026-03/EPC218-23%20v1.1%202026%20Verification%20Of%20Payee%20Scheme%20Rulebook_0.pdf) moved to version 1.1. It was an urgent release, fixing problems that surfaced once the service went live.

In Britain the Payment Systems Regulator is [consulting on removing the expiry date](https://www.psr.org.uk/media/ugtogbad/cp26-2-extending-specific-direction-17-july-2026.pdf) from the direction that requires Confirmation of Payee, so the rule doesn’t lapse on 1 November. In the US the Federal Reserve sells banks [Payee Name Verification](https://www.frbservices.org/financial-services/multiservice-solutions/payee-name-verification), which checks a name against a routing and account number before the money goes.

The shared position is reasonable: checking the name on the account is fraud prevention. It is, for one kind of fraud. The trouble starts with the word the screen uses to report it.

## The check does what it says

Uptake isn’t in question. Over 320 payment service providers offer the check in the UK, more than 99% of firms initiating a Faster Payment now offer it, and over 2 million checks complete every day.

It works. Pay.UK found a 59% drop in claims for payments sent to the wrong account, and losses down between 20% and 40% for some types of fraud. The regulator adds that a transaction where the name doesn’t match is 25 times more likely to be fraudulent.

A mismatch is one of the strongest single signals in retail payments. The check surfaces it before the money moves, which is why I’m not arguing against it.

## What a match cannot tell you

The PSR’s own account of the rule is careful about the distinction. Confirmation of Payee “was introduced to stop misdirected payments”. Then: “There was also an expectation that it would reduce the number of authorised push payment (APP) scams.”

The first happened. The second hasn’t shown up in the totals. [UK Finance reported](https://www.ukfinance.org.uk/news-and-insight/press-release/fraud-report-2026-press-release) £576.4 million lost to authorized push payment fraud in 2025, up 19%, across 248,070 cases. Banks reimbursed £354.3 million of it, about 61%.

No causal claim there. The reason the check can’t reach those scams is in the mechanism, not the rollout.

The check compares the name the payer typed with the name on the account. When someone is being talked into a payment, the same person supplies both. The fake seller gives you the name on the real account they control. The invoice arrives with new details on a letterhead you know. Both sides of the comparison come from the fraudster, so the check agrees with them.

The Federal Reserve is careful about this in its own marketing copy. Its service “may help to reduce the occurrences of Authorized Push Payment fraud where an imposter is impersonating an individual”. May help. Impersonating an individual. That’s one scam, not the category.

## The rulebook stops at the screen

The European rulebook runs to 68 pages and it’s precise where it needs to be. A responding provider returns one of five outcomes: match, no match, close match with the counterparty’s actual name, identification code not supported or verification not possible.

Then it says this about the person: “It should be noted that the way the Requester is informed and the content of the notification messages are left to the discretion of the Requesting PSP.”

So the machine-to-machine part is specified to the field. The part a human reads is a matter of taste. Sixty-eight pages on the message, one sentence on the screen.

## The wording carries the liability

This isn’t a copy quibble, because the European regulation already attached money to that screen. On a mismatch the payer’s provider must say that authorizing the transfer “might lead to transferring the funds to a payment account not held by the payee indicated by the payer”.

The provider also may not stop the payer going ahead. And it has to explain “the implications for PSP liability and PSU refund rights resulting from a decision by PSUs to ignore a notification”.

Read that in order. The bank warns you, can’t stop you, and your refund rights change if you continue. The sentence deciding all of that’s being written by whoever owns the string file.

## Two things I would hold the screen to

The first is a labeling rule. A check gets named for what it checked, so “this account is in the name you typed” is true and boring. “Payee verified” is a claim about the payment, and it’s the screen a fraudster wants glowing behind their phone call. A name check is a fact about an account, not a judgment about a person.

The second is the no-match state, which needs something to do. Today, in [RedCompass Labs’ summary](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/verification-payee-arrivesin-europe-6-big-lessons-redcompass-swnqe) of European go-live, the payer “can either proceed, amend, or stop the payment altogether”. Three doors and no help choosing between them, at the exact moment somebody may be on the phone explaining which one to pick.

My question in review is always the same. What can this person do in the next 10 seconds, and does the screen still work if they’re being coached while they read it?

I got that from the expensive end. At Best Egg I redesigned document verification so an applicant sees a status the moment a file lands, and the opportunity we sized was 7,000 fewer support calls a month. A status that doesn’t say what happens next produces a phone call. On a payment screen it produces a payment.

At Auth0 the same lesson arrived in a different vocabulary. A check that returns true is an engineering result. Turning it into “verified” is a product decision, and it’s usually made by nobody in particular.

Europe will run this check on every euro credit transfer. Britain looks set to keep its version for good, and the Fed is selling one by the transaction. None of the three specifies what the payer reads. That leaves the most load-bearing word in the flow to whoever writes it, which today is a designer working without a rulebook.

Sources:

- [Verification Of Payee Scheme Rulebook](https://www.europeanpaymentscouncil.eu/sites/default/files/kb/file/2026-03/EPC218-23%20v1.1%202026%20Verification%20Of%20Payee%20Scheme%20Rulebook_0.pdf)
- [Regulation (EU) 2024/886](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=OJ:L_202400886)
- [CP26/2: Specific Direction 17 (Confirmation of Payee)](https://www.psr.org.uk/media/ugtogbad/cp26-2-extending-specific-direction-17-july-2026.pdf)
- [Annual Fraud Report 2026](https://www.ukfinance.org.uk/news-and-insight/press-release/fraud-report-2026-press-release)
- [Payee Name Verification](https://www.frbservices.org/financial-services/multiservice-solutions/payee-name-verification)
- [Verification of Payee arrives in Europe: 6 big lessons](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/verification-payee-arrivesin-europe-6-big-lessons-redcompass-swnqe)

## Count the drift, not the adoption rate

- URL: https://john-desouza.com/blog/count-the-drift-not-the-adoption-rate.html
- Author: John DeSouza
- Published: 2026-09-26
- Topic: Design leadership
- Claim: A design system team earns its staffing on the count of what the system failed to prevent, not on an adoption rate or an estimate of hours saved.

Stakeholder buy-in for design systems dropped 10 points in a year and dissatisfaction nearly doubled. The advice going around is to build a better business case. Only 5% of teams measure the return they would be making that case from.

Satisfaction with stakeholder buy-in for design systems fell to 32% this year, down from 42%. The share of practitioners calling themselves dissatisfied went from 23% to 40%. Both numbers come from [zeroheight’s fifth annual report](https://report.zeroheight.com/), which surveyed 147 people who run a design system.

In the same survey, 56% named a lack of resourcing or staffing as their biggest problem. So the people holding the budget are less convinced than they were, and the teams have fewer people than they need.

## The answer the field reached for

The field’s answer is to get better at the business case. Figma’s [new business case for design systems](https://www.figma.com/blog/the-new-business-case-for-design-systems/), published in January, argues that systems “have evolved from static libraries to key drivers of business revenue, customer loyalty, and product strategy”. It comes with receipts. Freshworks cut customer service costs 28%. Grammarly saved its design and development teams 25% of a work week.

That’s a fair position. I’d rather a design system lead walked into a budget review talking about revenue than about component counts.

The trouble is sitting in the other half of the zeroheight report. Only 5% of teams measure return on investment at all. Just 41% track adoption. The field is being told to argue from evidence most of it has never collected.

So the case gets built out of somebody else’s numbers. Freshworks did the work and published it, and the slide borrows it. Nobody in your finance review is funding your team on Grammarly’s week.

## The hours nobody followed

[Shane P Williams put the sharpest version of this](https://designsystemscollective.substack.com/p/the-hours-came-back-nobody-asked) on September 14. Teams are good at counting the hours a system gives back and bad at saying where those hours went. “Two thousand reclaimed hours is only a win if you can name what they bought,” he writes. If they went into shipping more of the same, faster, “then what the system funded is volume”.

He’s right, and I’d push it one step further back. Most teams can’t name what the hours bought because they never had the hours. The saving came out of a spreadsheet, not a measurement.

And when a team does go and measure, the first number they reach for is the one that hides the problem.

## Adoption rate is a flattering number

Adoption answers one question: are people using our components. That’s the number a system team hopes to see, which is most of the reason it gets picked.

It’s also the number the tools hand you. The report found measurement scattered across Figma analytics, surveys, code repository tracking and spreadsheets, with 37% of teams using Figma analytics. Adoption is what comes out of the box, so adoption is what gets reported.

When I [measured our library at Best Egg](https://john-desouza.com/work/agentic-design-system-audit.html), adoption came back at 90.7% across 1.15 million instances in 296 files. Read on its own, that number says the work is finished.

The same audit found 844,333 values hand-set in files where a published token was sitting right there, unwired. It found 770 components with zero instances. Half the standalone library turned out to be illustrations that every designer scrolls past on the way to a button.

Adoption was 90.7% and the library still cost the team something every day. One of those numbers is an argument for leaving us alone. The other is an argument for funding us.

## Count the drift

Drift is what the system failed to prevent. It’s countable, and it’s the only design system number I have watched change a staffing conversation.

- **Hand-set values that already have a token.** Every one is a decision the system was supposed to have made for somebody.
- **Components with no instances.** Maintenance you pay for that sits unused.
- **Ties the data can’t break.** The value 10px appeared 1,834 times in our files and 12px 1,796. Nothing in the counts picks one. A person has to, and that person costs money.

A number like 844,333 does something an adoption rate can’t. It hands the person holding the budget a quantity they can multiply by a cost, and it names the work that would bring it down.

## Make the number harder to like

My test for a measurement is whether it can embarrass me.

Ours nearly wasn’t. The adoption formula had a name-match heuristic in it, counting a layer as on-system when its name looked close enough to a real component. I took it out. I excluded the archives and the library’s own file, and reported Brand Studio separately, because marketing collateral doesn’t instance a dropdown.

Every one of those choices pushed my own number down. That’s the point. An adoption rate that only ever goes up is a marketing asset, and the people reading it can tell.

The other half of the test is the calendar. The audit runs again on the first of every month, so drift has a trend and not a snapshot. One reading is a claim. Twelve of them is a line on a chart, and a line is what survives a budget review full of people who don’t design.

## Where the 56% comes from

Put the two findings next to each other. Resourcing is the top challenge, named by 56% of teams. Return on investment is measured by 5%.

Those are the same fact. Design system teams are asking for headcount in a currency they never minted. The business case advice isn’t wrong. It’s out of order. Instrument the thing, find out what it’s failing to prevent, and the case is yours instead of borrowed.

Seven percent of the teams in that survey report full adoption. Another 22% say the system reaches few teams. Somewhere in the gap between those two lines is a number with a dollar sign on it, and only about one team in 20 has gone and counted it.

Sources:

- [Design Systems Report 2026](https://report.zeroheight.com/)
- [The new business case for design systems](https://www.figma.com/blog/the-new-business-case-for-design-systems/)
- [The hours came back. Nobody asked where they went.](https://designsystemscollective.substack.com/p/the-hours-came-back-nobody-asked)
- [Agentic design system audit and remediation](/work/agentic-design-system-audit.html)

## Prototypes that cannot fail are demos

- URL: https://john-desouza.com/blog/prototypes-that-cannot-fail-are-demos.html
- Author: John DeSouza
- Published: 2026-09-25
- Topic: Where product design is going
- Claim: The cost of a high fidelity prototype used to force a team to name the question before the build. Now that the cost is gone, the question has to be written down on purpose, or the prototype is just a demo with a review on the calendar.

Forty-three percent of designers say their company expects a working prototype as the deliverable. Cheap fidelity was supposed to buy earlier answers. For most teams it bought an artifact nobody can argue with.

Jakob Nielsen made the case in [Vibe Coding and Vibe Design](https://jakobnielsenphd.substack.com/p/vibe-coding-vibe-design), quoting a line from Kshitij Agrawal that the field has more or less adopted.

mockups existed because coding was difficult; now that coding is easy, the future is prototypes

Kshitij Agrawal, quoted by Jakob Nielsen, March 2025

Go straight to something that runs. Test the real interaction instead of a picture of it. I agree with all of that. The conclusion skips a step, and the step it skips is the one that made prototypes work.

A high fidelity prototype used to cost about a week of somebody’s time. That price did a job nobody assigned to it. It forced a conversation before the build, because no team spends a week without asking what the week is for. The question came first because the budget made it come first.

## The deliverable ate the question

Forty-three percent of designers say their company now expects a working prototype as the deliverable, according to [AI in Design 2026](https://stateofaidesign.com/chapters/craft), a survey of more than 900 designers in 60 countries. Half have pushed AI-generated code to production. In the [State of Prototyping](https://survey.uxtools.co/spring-2026) survey run by Tommy Geoco and UX Tools, 1,478 responses collected this spring, 43.8% now spend more than half their building time on code a model wrote.

A deliverable and a prototype have different jobs. A deliverable gets accepted. A prototype gets built to be wrong in a particular way that somebody named in advance, and the whole point is that it might come back wrong.

When the artifact arrives before the question, the question gets written afterward, if anyone writes it at all. A question written after the build is a rationalization with a sample size attached.

## What gets approved is average

Ninety-two people were shown AI-generated and human-made prototypes without being told which was which, and rated them on the short user experience questionnaire. The [results](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15124) split cleanly. Positive on the pragmatic side: usable, efficient, clear. Neutral to negative on originality and innovation. The authors called it usable but conventional.

Nielsen Norman Group ran their own version, rebuilding one of their training pages with three kinds of prompt. The detailed prompts got close to the human original. The outputs still [missed visual hierarchy, color contrast and consistent margins](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-prototyping/), which is why they land on these tools being better for ideation than for production.

So the thing showing up in your review is competent, conventional and finished-looking. All three at once is very hard to argue with. That’s the problem, not the achievement. In Figma’s [State of the Designer 2026](https://www.figma.com/blog/state-of-the-designer-2026/), 58% of designers define craft as visual polish, ahead of thoughtful problem solving at 47%. Polish is the part that just became free.

## One line at the top

Nothing goes into a design review without one line at the top of it: the belief this is built to kill, and what we would be looking at if that belief were wrong.

I want that line before the build, not in the deck afterward. If nobody on the team can write it, we’re building a demo, and I’d rather we call it a demo and put it on the calendar as one. Demos are useful. They’re just not evidence.

The first question in the review is the same question. What would this look like if we were wrong? If the honest answer is “about the same”, the prototype tested nothing and the next 40 minutes are a conversation about taste. Sometimes that’s the meeting you needed. It shouldn’t be the meeting you thought you were having.

At Best Egg, applicants uploaded their documents and then the dashboard went quiet. What we were testing was whether telling them the status after the upload changed how many finished, not whether the screen looked better. That version of the question has a result. It went through an A/B test before rollout and came back with one.

## The forcing function has to come from a person now

Eighty percent of designers say they still rely on their own quality meter over the model’s. I believe them, and I don’t think a quality meter is the thing under threat here. Judgment about whether a screen is good survives cheap production fine.

What doesn’t survive is the part of the process that used to happen on its own because building was expensive. Somebody named the uncertainty. The team agreed ahead of time on what a bad result would look like. And before anyone opened a tool, everyone knew which of the plausible directions the build was there to rule out.

None of that was ever a method. It was a side effect of the price, and the price is gone. Which means it’s now somebody’s job, in writing, or it doesn’t happen.

The teams that get this wrong aren’t going to look slow. They’re going to look extremely fast, and they’re going to ship a lot of usable, conventional, well-spaced work that nobody in the building ever had the standing to question.

Sources:

- [Craft, AI in Design 2026](https://stateofaidesign.com/chapters/craft)
- [State of Prototyping: Spring 2026](https://survey.uxtools.co/spring-2026)
- [Usable but Conventional](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15124)
- [AI Prototyping in Real Design Contexts](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-prototyping/)
- [Vibe Coding and Vibe Design](https://jakobnielsenphd.substack.com/p/vibe-coding-vibe-design)
- [State of the Designer 2026](https://www.figma.com/blog/state-of-the-designer-2026/)

## Train juniors on what they reject

- URL: https://john-desouza.com/blog/train-juniors-on-what-they-reject.html
- Author: John DeSouza
- Published: 2026-09-24
- Topic: Design leadership
- Claim: AI makes a junior’s output look senior long before their judgment is, so the unit of training has to move from what they produce to what they reject and why.

The case for hiring junior designers again is winning this month. The case for how to train them is barely being made, and the study usually cited for it measured speed, not judgment.

The junior designer argument came around again this week, from both sides. On Tuesday [Patrick Neeman made the case](https://aiforux.substack.com/p/the-ux-field-survives-on-leaders) that the field survives on leaders who keep hiring juniors, because every senior designer was once a bet somebody made. On Wednesday [CNBC quoted](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/23/ai-workplace-graduate-entry-level-junior-hiring.html) Tobias Green, founder of the London ad agency Catalyst, making the opposite case: “If AI removes the grunt work, then the grunt work is no longer relevant.”

I’m with Neeman on the hire. I think both of them have the training wrong.

## Hiring them is the easy half

The hiring numbers aren’t subtle. In [Figma’s 2026 hiring study](https://www.figma.com/blog/why-demand-for-designers-is-on-the-rise/), 56% of hiring managers reported rising demand for senior designers. Only 25% were hiring for junior roles. A [working paper from two Harvard researchers](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5425555) tracked 62 million workers at 285,000 American firms through their résumés. Junior employment fell sharply at companies that adopted generative AI, while senior employment barely moved. The drop came from slower hiring, not from people being let go.

Nobody announced the end of junior hiring. The requisitions just stopped getting opened. Neeman’s answer is to open the requisition anyway, and he is right. Every senior designer was a junior somewhere first.

The weak part of his argument is the reason he gives for why now is a good time. He cites the Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond study of support agents, where novices with an AI assistant improved 34% and the most experienced barely changed. His conclusion is that the tools compress the time it takes a new person to become useful.

## Useful is not the same as trained

Look at what [that study](https://www.nber.org/papers/w31161) measured: issues resolved per hour. It’s an output number. The authors’ own explanation is that the model “disseminates the best practices of more able workers” to the new ones. The novices got faster because they were carrying someone else’s practice, not because they had formed their own.

That’s fine in a support queue. In a design team it switches off the oldest signal a lead has. A junior who needed help used to show it in the work: the muddled hierarchy, the empty state nobody drew, the flow that fell apart on the third screen. Weak output was the alarm.

Now a junior with a good model hands in a competent screen in their first week. It looks like progress. It might be. Or the model did the part that used to teach them, and they approved it.

Cheney Hamilton of the research firm Bloor named the gap in the same CNBC piece. AI raises what a junior can produce, she said, but it “doesn’t give them the judgement to know when the output is wrong”. That judgment came from repetition and consequence, and those are exactly the parts the tool now absorbs.

## The player-coach has no time for screens

The standard answer is that seniors will teach the judgment on purpose. The org chart is moving the other way. In May [Coinbase cut about 14% of its staff](https://www.coinbase.com/blog/building-a-leaner-and-faster-coinbase) and capped the company at five layers below the chief executive and chief operating officer. Leaders would carry as many as 15 or more direct reports. There are no pure managers left. Every leader is also meant to be an active individual contributor.

A player-coach with 15 reports and their own work to ship can’t sit beside a junior and critique every frame. A [small interview study of software engineers in South Korea](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17067) gave the pattern a name: absorption. Entry-level work gets pulled into senior workflows running on AI, and juniors skip the struggle that used to build expertise. The seniors and juniors it interviewed didn’t even see the problem the same way.

So the training has to happen somewhere cheaper than a screen-by-screen review. And it has to leave a trace a busy lead can read.

## What I review instead

In my reviews, a junior’s work comes with what they threw away. The options the model gave them that they killed, and one line on why each one died, written against the team’s standard.

I read the reasons before I look at the screen. The order matters, because it separates two juniors who hand in the same competent work.

- **Right reasons, rough screen.** That’s a craft gap. It closes with practice, and the tools help.
- **Polished screen, thin reasons.** The model got it right and the junior agreed. That’s where my time goes, because nothing in the output would have told me.

None of this works unless the standard is written down. A junior can’t explain why an option fails an unstated bar, and a lead can’t check the explanation against a mood. Adam Elman made a related case about AI products at [Nielsen Norman Group in June](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-era-critique/): the designer’s job shifts toward defining what good does and doesn’t look like.

The rejection notes also test the standard. Where it has gaps, they show up as reasons the team can’t give.

And it gives the review a unit a player-coach can afford. A paragraph of reasons can be read between meetings. A file full of frames can’t.

## The grunt work was never the point

Green is right that nobody should keep juniors on busywork for its own sake. He is wrong that the skill it built stopped mattering. Grunt work taught judgment because every piece of it came back with a verdict. Somebody said no, and said why.

A model rarely tells a junior no. It hands them another option. The only person left to say no is the junior, and the only way to know whether they can is to have them do it in writing, where someone will read it.

So hire the junior, and review what they reject.

Sources:

- [The UX Field Survives on Leaders Who Hire Juniors To Learn AI](https://aiforux.substack.com/p/the-ux-field-survives-on-leaders)
- [AI at work: Companies rethink entry-level, graduate and junior hiring](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/23/ai-workplace-graduate-entry-level-junior-hiring.html)
- [Why demand for designers is on the rise](https://www.figma.com/blog/why-demand-for-designers-is-on-the-rise/)
- [Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5425555)
- [Generative AI at Work](https://www.nber.org/papers/w31161)
- [Building a leaner and faster Coinbase](https://www.coinbase.com/blog/building-a-leaner-and-faster-coinbase)
- [Who Will Become the Next Senior?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17067)
- [The Core Skill of Design in the AI Era: Critique](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-era-critique/)

## Your design system checks spelling, not judgment

- URL: https://john-desouza.com/blog/design-systems-check-spelling-not-judgment.html
- Author: John DeSouza
- Published: 2026-09-24
- Topic: Where product design is going
- Claim: Machine-readable design systems enforce the vocabulary and drop the judgment, and the judgment only gets written down if every rejected answer leaves a reason behind.

This year the design system became the thing the model reads. Almost all of the work went into making sure an agent uses a real button. Almost none went into whether it should have used a button at all.

The design system is now the thing the model reads. In a [July survey of 21 open-source design systems](https://state-of-ai-in-design-systems.netlify.app/), Kaelig Deloumeau-Prigent found that 18 ship an official MCP server so coding agents can query them directly. Figma describes its new agent as having [“deep context on your components, tokens, standards, and best practices”](https://www.figma.com/blog/the-figma-agent-is-here/).

The position behind all of this is reasonable. Give the agent your system and it builds on your system. The components and tokens become the guardrail, and on-brand output follows.

I think that gets the guardrail half right and drops the half that matters.

## What the machine-readable half enforces

The same survey catalogs 165 techniques teams use to keep models on their real components and tokens. The biggest groups are validation loops (31), prohibitions like “never invent components” (28), tool-gating that makes a fake component impossible to produce (22) and token enforcement that fails the build on a raw hex value (15).

That’s serious engineering, and it works. It also has a clear shape. Most of them answer one question: is this a real part of the system, used the way its API allows?

That’s spelling. An agent can pass all of it and still put a primary button in every row of a table, because every one of those buttons is a real button with a real token.

## The part that got cut first

Atlassian tested Google’s DESIGN.md format against its own MCP server and skills and wrote up what happened. To fit the design system into one portable file, the team says it [“had to remove much of the usage guidance from our 50+ components”](https://www.atlassian.com/blog/how-we-build/atlassians-design-md-is-here-what-we-learned-testing-portable-design-context-in-practice). Agents given the file then went digging through component code to find the guidance that was missing.

Usage guidance is where the judgment lives. It’s the paragraph that says when not to use the thing. Nord, one of the systems in the survey, ships it to agents in exactly that form: [“Don’t use a primary button in every row of a table.”](https://nordhealth.design/.well-known/skills/nord/references/components/button.md) No linter catches that sentence being ignored. It’s also what went first when Atlassian needed the file smaller.

Tokens are cheap to write down. They’re values with names. The reasons behind the choices are expensive, and the reasons are the part a designer was actually hired to supply.

## Frequency is not a standard

When an agent has no reason to go on, it falls back on what’s common. Figma says its agent [“uses your most frequently and recently used components as a starting point”](https://www.figma.com/blog/the-figma-agent-is-here/). That’s a sensible default for a tool and a poor definition of good.

I have seen why. When I ran an agent audit across a whole design library, I wrote the crawler’s rules, and it counted every value we had. It couldn’t tell me which of two established values was right. Somebody had to decide, and the decision was nowhere in the data.

Nurkhon Akhmedov puts the failure mode well in [a July post on this](https://nurxmedov.substack.com/p/your-design-systems-real-job-in-2026): five screens in a hundred ship off-system, and “the next agent reads those five as if they were the library.” A system that learns from its own output drifts toward whatever it did most, right or wrong.

## Gated on spelling, trusted on judgment

The survey also looked for whether teams measure any of this. [Eight of the 21 records mention evaluation work at all](https://state-of-ai-in-design-systems.netlify.app/questions/evals.md). The report calls its validation loops the closest thing the field has, and describes them as “checks that fail a build, rather than evals that score a model.”

So the mechanical half is gated and the judgment half is trusted. Akhmedov’s version is blunter: whether the agent picked the right component for what the user is trying to do is a question “you can’t grep for.”

## Where the missing half comes from

Akhmedov argues the rubric is now the deliverable. I agree, and I’d go one step further on where it comes from.

Nobody writes good usage guidance in the abstract. Try to list every wrong way to use a button in advance and you get a style guide nobody reads. The useful rules show up one at a time, when someone looks at a screen an agent built and says no.

That moment is the raw material, and it’s easy to lose. The rejection happens in a review, the agent gets a new prompt, the screen gets fixed and the reason lives in one person’s head until they leave.

A rejection without a written reason is wasted. The reason goes into the system the agent reads, in the form Nord already uses: the choice that was wrong, the one that was right and why. Written that way, the next agent can be held to it and so can the next designer.

## What the design system team is for now

For years the visible output of a design system team was the library. This year the industry made that library readable and enforceable for agents. That work was worth doing.

It was also the easy half. A system that only knows its own vocabulary will produce fluent, valid, wrong screens at whatever speed you let it. The half that decides whether a screen is right is still mostly sitting in people’s heads, and in at least one case it was trimmed out on purpose to make a file fit.

Sources:

- [State of AI in Design Systems, July 2026](https://state-of-ai-in-design-systems.netlify.app/)
- [Does anyone measure whether their AI affordances work?](https://state-of-ai-in-design-systems.netlify.app/questions/evals.md)
- [Atlassian's DESIGN.md is here](https://www.atlassian.com/blog/how-we-build/atlassians-design-md-is-here-what-we-learned-testing-portable-design-context-in-practice)
- [The Figma agent is here](https://www.figma.com/blog/the-figma-agent-is-here/)
- [Nord button reference](https://nordhealth.design/.well-known/skills/nord/references/components/button.md)
- [Your design system's real job in 2026 is catching the AI](https://nurxmedov.substack.com/p/your-design-systems-real-job-in-2026)

## Stablecoin trust is decided at redemption

- URL: https://john-desouza.com/blog/stablecoin-trust-is-decided-at-redemption.html
- Author: John DeSouza
- Published: 2026-09-24
- Topic: Fintech, web3 and trust
- Claim: Rewards decide whether people move money into a stablecoin. Redemption decides whether they trust it, and the draft rules have already written a bad day that the rewards fight ignores.

The Clarity Act, and the Senate fight over stablecoin rewards with it, stalled 49 to 50 last week. Meanwhile the draft federal rule already spells out what happens when too many people ask for their dollars back at once, and almost no one in that fight is talking about the screen those people will see.

On September 15 the Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act, [49 to 50](https://www.americanbanker.com/news/crypto-market-structure-bill-fails-in-senate-vote-49-50). American Banker called the extent to which stablecoin companies could offer yield-like products the leading issue of the debate. The day before, [eight banking groups](https://www.coindesk.com/policy/2026/09/14/banks-escalate-stablecoin-rewards-fight-as-senate-prepares-for-a-clarity-act-vote) were still pushing for tighter limits on rewards, arguing they work like deposit interest.

Within three days, two Substack writers read the same failure in opposite directions. [Anndy Lian](https://anndy.substack.com/p/clarity-act-diesstablecoin-yields) headlined that stablecoin yields survive. [Andrew Dresner](https://paymentsinfull.substack.com/p/how-does-claritys-failure-impact) argued the failure counts as a win for banks, because the tighter GENIUS Act restrictions now govern.

Both sides share one assumption, and it’s a fair one: what a person earns for holding a stablecoin decides whether they move money into it. I agree with it. It’s still the wrong screen to fight over.

## The bad day is already written down

The GENIUS Act already bans issuers from paying holders [any form of interest or yield](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ27/html/PLAW-119publ27.htm) in section 4(a)(11). Section 4 also requires a public redemption policy with procedures for “timely redemption”. The statute never says how timely. The regulators do.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) proposed its rule in March. [Its section 15.12](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/03/02/2026-04089/implementing-the-guiding-and-establishing-national-innovation-for-us-stablecoins-act-for-the) puts timely at two business days. Then it defines the bad day. If redemption requests pass 10% of an issuer’s outstanding issuance in a single 24-hour period, the window becomes seven calendar days. That applies to every request already in line and every one after it. Only the OCC can shorten it, and the OCC can also extend it further.

The rule is defensible. Regulators need some way to slow a run, and compliance isn’t the problem here.

The problem is what the person sees. Section 15.12 has the issuer notify the OCC within 24 hours. What it asks the issuer to tell holders is a statement in the redemption policy explaining when the period can stretch. So the one moment a stablecoin behaves least like a dollar is covered by a paragraph on a policy page.

## Mechanism, labeled as transparency

The disclosures the law does require are real and useful. Once the law takes effect, an issuer publishes its outstanding supply every month, along with the composition of its reserves, down to the average tenor and where each category of reserve is held. The OCC’s draft puts a link to that report in the same disclosure as the fees.

That report is for analysts. A person holding stablecoins in an app has one question on the bad day: when does my money land, and what would make it later? A reserve breakdown answers a different question, and putting it on the screen is how the industry keeps exposing its machinery and calling it transparency.

It gets harder, because a person holding a stablecoin in an exchange app may never deal with the issuer at all. As [Liam Wright wrote in CryptoSlate](https://cryptoslate.com/proposed-stablecoin-rules-might-guarantee-your-dollar-while-making-you-wait-a-week-to-spend-it/) on the day of the vote, a faster exit depends on the service converting the coin, which has to pay out before the issuer pays it. So the wait a person feels is set by whoever sits between them and the issuer. That’s the same kind of platform whose rewards the Senate just fought over.

## The states a balance can be in

Read the statute as a product spec and a stablecoin balance can be in four states a rewards banner never mentions. Each one needs a screen.

- **Pending.** Redemption requested, due within two business days under the draft rule.
- **Extended.** The 10% line was crossed by other people, and the person’s own request now waits seven days.
- **Frozen.** Issuers must be able to seize, freeze, burn or block transfer of coins under a [lawful order](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ27/html/PLAW-119publ27.htm), section 4(a)(6)(B).
- **In insolvency.** Holders get priority on the required reserves, and section 11 asks the bankruptcy court to use best efforts to begin distributions within 14 days of the hearing.

The extended state is the one that should worry product teams. Nothing the person did caused it, and nothing on a normal balance screen would explain it.

## Lending already paid for this lesson

At Best Egg, loan applicants uploaded their documents and then the dashboard went quiet. Nothing said whether a file was pending, accepted or still needed, so they called to ask. We replaced it with a [status for every document](https://john-desouza.com/work/verifications.html), sized at 7,000 fewer support calls a month.

Stablecoin redemption is that screen with the person’s own money behind it. A silent “processing” on day four of a seven-day extension doesn’t read as a rule working as designed. It reads as a freeze. [Jayson Derrick](https://crypto-compass-daily.beehiiv.com/p/the-redemption-cliff-how-the-occ-s-10-percent-trigger-turns-a-routine-withdrawal-wave-into-a-seven-d) wrote about the trigger in May and pictured retail holders opening their apps on a Sunday night to find “a locked gate.” That’s the screen to draw first.

## The screen I ask for first

Put a stablecoin product in front of me and the first screen I’d ask for is the balance on day four of an extended redemption. What does it say happened, what does it say happens next and on what date?

If the team shows me the rewards rate instead, the product has been designed for the day money arrives and not for the day it tries to leave.

Comptroller Jonathan Gould said in August that the OCC wants [a final rule out by November](https://www.theblock.co/news/regulation/2026-08-19-occ-races-to-finalize-genius-act-stablecoin-rules-by-november-412240). Under section 20 the law takes effect no later than January 18, 2027. The rewards fight, American Banker reports, starts over in the next Congress. The redemption screen gets built before then either way.

Sources:

- [Public Law 119-27, the GENIUS Act](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ27/html/PLAW-119publ27.htm)
- [OCC proposed rule implementing the GENIUS Act](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/03/02/2026-04089/implementing-the-guiding-and-establishing-national-innovation-for-us-stablecoins-act-for-the)
- [Crypto market structure bill fails in Senate vote, 49-50](https://www.americanbanker.com/news/crypto-market-structure-bill-fails-in-senate-vote-49-50)
- [Banks escalate stablecoin rewards fight as Senate prepares for a Clarity Act vote](https://www.coindesk.com/policy/2026/09/14/banks-escalate-stablecoin-rewards-fight-as-senate-prepares-for-a-clarity-act-vote)
- [How does Clarity's failure impact stablecoins](https://paymentsinfull.substack.com/p/how-does-claritys-failure-impact)
- [CLARITY Act dies, stablecoin yields survive](https://anndy.substack.com/p/clarity-act-diesstablecoin-yields)
- [Proposed stablecoin rules might guarantee your dollar while making you wait a week to spend it](https://cryptoslate.com/proposed-stablecoin-rules-might-guarantee-your-dollar-while-making-you-wait-a-week-to-spend-it/)
- [The redemption cliff](https://crypto-compass-daily.beehiiv.com/p/the-redemption-cliff-how-the-occ-s-10-percent-trigger-turns-a-routine-withdrawal-wave-into-a-seven-d)
- [OCC races to finalize GENIUS Act stablecoin rules by November](https://www.theblock.co/news/regulation/2026-08-19-occ-races-to-finalize-genius-act-stablecoin-rules-by-november-412240)

## Metered pulls make frequency a consent question

- URL: https://john-desouza.com/blog/frequency-is-a-consent-question.html
- Author: John DeSouza
- Published: 2026-09-24
- Topic: Fintech, web3 and trust
- Claim: Once every data pull has a price, how often an app checks a bank account stops being a back-end setting. It’s a consent decision, and it belongs on the consent screen instead of an invoice.

JPMorgan Chase already bills aggregators for every data request, and the rewrite of the open banking rule is expected to let other banks follow. The argument is about who pays. The screen where a person finds out how often an app looks at their account has barely been designed.

JPMorgan Chase now charges data aggregators like Plaid for the requests its systems answer. The fee applies to each call rather than a monthly total, a JPMorgan managing director [told a panel in December](https://www.paymentsdive.com/news/open-banking-fees-fintechs-fuel-debate-cfpb-apps/808114/). The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s rewrite of the Section 1033 open banking rule [went to the White House for review in August](https://www.consumerfinancemonitor.com/2026/08/06/cfpb-sends-new-section-1033-open-banking-proposal-to-oira-for-review/), and it is [expected to let banks charge](https://www.americanbanker.com/news/what-we-know-about-the-cfpbs-forthcoming-open-banking-rule) for access the 2024 version made free.

The fight is being argued as a question of who pays. The Financial Technology Association [says](https://www.ftassociation.org/looking-ahead-to-the-open-banking-rule-protecting-americans-right-to-securely-access-and-share-their-financial-data-without-fees/) the costs “will be passed directly on to American consumers and small businesses,” and that data access is a legal entitlement, “not a conditional right contingent upon paying access fees.” That’s a serious argument about competition. This post doesn’t argue the price.

It argues about the screen, because a price changes what the screen is for.

## Both sides agree the product sets the volume

Listen to what each side says about volume and they land in the same place. On that December panel, JPMorgan’s Kate Prochaska said: “Once people actually have to pay for things, they start thinking about, ‘Well, do I need to ping this often?‘” The association’s Angelena Bradfield answered that how much data an app pulls is a function of the user’s experience. People check their apps, and the app checks the bank.

PNC put the bank case more bluntly in its comment letter to the bureau, [as quoted by Payments Dive](https://www.paymentsdive.com/news/open-banking-fees-fintechs-fuel-debate-cfpb-apps/808114/): “When third party access to consumer data is free and unlimited, third parties have little incentive to minimize cadence, scope, or retention of data they do not need and will not use.”

One side calls the volume waste. The other calls it the product working. Both are saying that how often an app looks at a bank account is a product decision. Neither has said where the person whose account it’s gets to see that decision.

## Frequency was never on the screen

The 2024 rule came closer than anything before it. It told apps to limit collection to what is “reasonably necessary” for the product the person asked for, and it [defined collection](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/11/18/2024-25079/required-rulemaking-on-personal-financial-data-rights) to include “the scope of covered data requested and the duration and frequency of collection.” It capped every authorization at one year before the app had to ask again.

Now look at what the same rule required the person to be shown. The authorization disclosure lists the app, the bank, the product, the categories of data and the expected duration. Frequency isn’t on the list. The one variable a bank can now put a price on is the one the strictest version of the rule never asked anyone to show.

That rule isn’t in force either. A federal court in Kentucky [has blocked enforcement](https://www.cozen.com/news-resources/publications/2026/section-1033-compliance-date-open-banking-rule-enjoined-and-under-reconsideration) while the bureau reconsiders it, and the [reconsideration notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/08/22/2025-16139/personal-financial-data-rights-reconsideration) asks whether banks should be able to “recover a reasonable rate” for answering requests.

## The invoice decides if the screen doesn’t

Today the answer to “how often” lives on a signup screen nobody reads twice. CNBC reported an internal JPMorgan memo complaining that aggregators access data “multiple times daily, even when the customer is not actively using the app.” Plaid’s [answer](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/07/28/jpmorgan-fintech-middlemen-plaid-data-requests-taxing-systems.html) was that all of that activity begins with the permission a customer grants at signup, and that background calls are how people get “critical alerts for overdraft fees or suspicious activity.”

Plaid is right that those alerts matter. That’s the problem. The pull that catches an overdraft is the same kind of pull a bank now bills for, and the person who wanted the alert agreed to it with one tap that never mentioned it.

So far the meter has stayed out of sight. When Plaid and JPMorgan renewed their agreement, Plaid told clients that [current contracts and customer fees remain unchanged](https://finovate.com/jpmorgans-data-access-agreement-from-plaids-perspective/). The cost sits in a contract between two companies, and JPMorgan says the trimming has started there: once it announced fees, Prochaska said, “people are more judicious and thoughtful about it.”

If a balance that used to refresh in the background starts refreshing only when the app opens, the overdraft warning arrives after the overdraft. Nobody chose that on a screen. It got chosen in a contract. That’s the failure state worth worrying about, and it isn’t a breach. It’s a downgrade the person never agreed to and has no way to see.

## Identity already has a word for this

OpenID Connect, the identity layer under most modern login flows, treats access while you’re away as its own grant. The spec defines an [offline_access scope](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html) and says the provider “MUST always obtain consent” before issuing the token that allows it. It adds that “a previously saved user consent is not always sufficient,” because access when the user isn’t present poses greater privacy risk.

At Auth0 I worked inside that model, where consent is granted scope by scope and each scope has a name. Open banking consent still bundles “while I’m using the app” and “while I’m asleep” into a single tap. Identity split those two apart years ago, and a price per pull is a good reason for open banking to do the same.

## What the screen should say

The lazy version of this screen is a number. “This app may request your data up to 12 times a day” is accurate, and it’s a mechanism dressed as a disclosure. You can’t make a decision with it.

The version a person can decide on names what the looking buys them and what stops if they say no. Check my balance in the background so you can warn me before an overdraft. Or only update when I open the app. Two choices, each with its consequence, and the app lives with whichever one the person picks.

That forces the product team to do what the price is already forcing on the business side: say which pulls are the product and which are habit. A pull that can’t be explained on that screen in one plain sentence is a pull the app should stop making.

The question I’d put to any background access in a design review is simple. What does the person get from us looking while they’re not here? If the team can’t answer in a sentence the person would recognize, the access goes, not the sentence.

Whatever the bureau publishes, the meter is already running at the largest bank in the country. Where the decision about how often gets made is still open. It can be made on the consent screen, where the person sees it, or in a contract they’ll never read.

Sources:

- [CFPB sends new Section 1033 open banking proposal to OIRA for review](https://www.consumerfinancemonitor.com/2026/08/06/cfpb-sends-new-section-1033-open-banking-proposal-to-oira-for-review/)
- [What we know about the CFPB's forthcoming open-banking rule](https://www.americanbanker.com/news/what-we-know-about-the-cfpbs-forthcoming-open-banking-rule)
- [Looking ahead to the open banking rule](https://www.ftassociation.org/looking-ahead-to-the-open-banking-rule-protecting-americans-right-to-securely-access-and-share-their-financial-data-without-fees/)
- [Required Rulemaking on Personal Financial Data Rights](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/11/18/2024-25079/required-rulemaking-on-personal-financial-data-rights)

- [JPMorgan says fintech middlemen like Plaid are 'massively taxing' its systems](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/07/28/jpmorgan-fintech-middlemen-plaid-data-requests-taxing-systems.html)

## Your team stopped taking your advice

- URL: https://john-desouza.com/blog/your-team-stopped-taking-your-advice.html
- Author: John DeSouza
- Published: 2026-09-22
- Topic: Design leadership
- Claim: You’re no longer the fastest source of useful knowledge on your team, and trying to win that back is the most expensive mistake available to you right now.

In one year, the number of designers learning from each other went from a quarter to more than two thirds. Over the same year, the number taking recommendations from their leadership fell by half. Both numbers describe the same shift.

Here are two numbers from [a survey](https://stateofaidesign.com/chapters/teams) of more than 900 designers. Peer learning went from 24% to 70% in a year. The share of designers taking recommendations from their leadership went from 32% to 16%.

The first number gets quoted constantly, usually as a feel-good line about community. The second one barely gets quoted at all, and it’s the one that should be keeping design leaders up.

## The comfortable reading is wrong

The comfortable reading is that this is a culture problem. Teams got scattered, people stopped looking up, leaders need to communicate better and be more present.

I don’t think that’s what happened. I think the method started turning over faster than any management chain can carry it.

The average designer’s toolstack went from three tools to seven in 12 months. When the useful knowledge has a shelf life measured in weeks, the person three levels up is structurally the last to hear it. Not because they’re disengaged. Because that’s what a hierarchy does to information that expires: it delays it.

Your team didn’t lose respect for you. They found a faster path, and they were right to take it.

## The expensive mistake

The expensive mistake is trying to win method authority back.

It looks reasonable from the inside. You block time, you learn the tools, you show up to the design review with a working prototype you built yourself. And it does buy you something real, which is that you stop being illegible to your own team.

But you can’t win that race. There are eight of them and one of you, they’re in the tools all day, and whatever you learn this quarter is half wrong by the next. Meanwhile the thing only you can do is sitting there not getting done.

I watch leaders spend their scarce hours becoming the fourth-best prototyper on a team of six. It’s the most sympathetic failure mode I know and it’s still a failure mode.

## Make the trade explicit

The trade I have settled on is that the team owns the method and I own the standard and the decision.

Owning the standard means I’m accountable for writing down what good means here, precisely enough that someone who wasn’t in the room can hold work to it. Not a mood, not a principle poster. The actual bar, in words, that a person or a model can be measured against.

Owning the decision means the calls that need a name on them stay with me. Which of two entrenched options we standardize on. What we deprecate when the data is tied. Anything where somebody’s work is on the other end of the answer.

When I audited our design library this year, the analysis came back saying one spacing value appeared 1,834 times and the competing one 1,796. Nothing in the data was ever going to break that tie. Somebody had to pick, say so out loud, and then go make the other one wrong. That isn’t a job you can delegate downward or automate, and it’s the job.

What I don’t do any more is pretend I know the best way to get from a brief to a prototype this month. They know. I ask.

## What this looks like on a calendar

Three things I actually changed, in case the principle is too tidy to be useful.

- **I ask what changed in your method, every one-on-one.** Not as a check-in, as intake. It’s how I find out what the team knows before the quarter is over. Half of what I now believe about working with agents came off that question.
- **Whoever found the better way presents it, not me.** The moment a leader relays somebody else’s discovery, two things break: the credit and the accuracy.
- **I write the standard down before anyone touches a tool.** If the team can’t say in a paragraph what a correct component looks like, no amount of tooling discovers it. It averages whatever is already there and hands it back with confidence.

## The part few leaders have done

The [same survey](https://designerfund.com/blog/ai-in-design-2026) found that only 28% of leaders made any formal change to evaluation, pay or hiring. Just 8% changed performance metrics and 4% touched compensation.

So the work changed, who people learn from changed, and what we reward stayed exactly where it was. That gap is where good designers quietly decide their leadership isn’t paying attention, and it’s a gap leaders can close without permission from anyone.

Start with the review template. If it still rewards volume of screens, it’s measuring the part of the job that got cheap.

The same report has 80% of designers still trusting their own quality judgment over the model’s. Taste didn’t go anywhere. What went is the assumption that it flows downhill from the person with the biggest title.

Sources:

- [AI in Design 2026](https://designerfund.com/blog/ai-in-design-2026)
- [Teams](https://stateofaidesign.com/chapters/teams)
- [Craft](https://stateofaidesign.com/chapters/craft)
